e.meaning: my God is an oath; pet form of Elizabeth
e.etymology: A pet form of Elizabeth. It was the childhood nickname of Queen Elizabeth II, who could not say her full name as a toddler, and was given to her great-granddaughter Princess Lilibet in 2021.
namesakes: Princess Lilibet of Sussex (daughter of Prince Harry and Meghan)

assoc.t: childhood nickname of Queen Elizabeth II

e.etymology: A spelling of Miral, a girls' name used in Arab and Pakistani families.
The English form of Homeros, the Greek poet credited with the Iliad and the Odyssey. The Greek word homeros means hostage, though whether that explains the name is unknown.

assoc.t: Homer Simpson, the father on The Simpsons
Homer, Greek poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey
homer, baseball slang for a home run

e.note: Most Americans think first of Homer Simpson and his catchphrase D'oh.

e.etymology: A form of Dinah or Dina, from Hebrew Dinah, judged. It has also been used as a short form of Deanna.
In the 1940s it was a girls' spelling of Karen, the Danish form of Katherine. Recent American use is for boys, where it sits with Daron, Jaron and Kamron.
A modern American name that joins the Sha- opening to the -niya ending of Aniya and Taniya. It also echoes Shania, made famous by the singer Shania Twain.
A spelling of Darian or Darien, names that took shape in 20th-century America beside Darius and Darren.
A modern American name built from the Ja- opening and the -miya sound of Amiya and Kamiya.
A variant of Evelyn, which began as an English surname from the medieval girls' name Aveline, brought by the Normans. This spelling is also the usual Dutch and French form.
A combination of Emma and Leigh, said like Emily. Emma is Germanic, from a word for whole or universal; Leigh is an English surname from Old English leah, a meadow or clearing.

e.meaning: a line of rulers from one family
e.etymology: The English word, used as a name. It comes through Latin from Greek dynasteia, power or lordship. Its use for girls followed the 1980s TV drama Dynasty.

assoc.t: Dynasty, 1980s prime-time TV soap and its 2017 remake

e.etymology: A spelling of Arabic Tariq, from taraqa, to knock: one who arrives by night, and a name for the morning star. Tariq ibn Ziyad, who crossed into Spain in 711, gave his name to Gibraltar.
namesakes: Tarek El Moussa (HGTV host of Flip or Flop)

e.etymology: From Greek Thais, the name of a companion of Alexander the Great and later of an Egyptian saint, the heroine of Massenet's opera. It is a popular name in Brazil.
e.note: Spelled the same as Thais, the people of Thailand, so it is often misread.

e.etymology: The initials T. J. written as a name. They usually stand for a first and middle name, or for a T name with Junior.
In American use it sits with Jamar and Lamar as a Ka- name. It also matches Arabic qamar, moon, a name usually written Qamar.

e.meaning: the twelfth month; Latin for tenth month
e.etymology: The month name, used as a given name. Latin december comes from decem, ten, because it was the tenth month of the early Roman calendar.

assoc.t: December, the last month of the year

e.etymology: The Yiddish form of Moshe, the Hebrew name of Moses. Exodus explains it as drawn out, because Pharaoh's daughter drew the infant from the Nile.
Usually explained as Hawaiian ka mea, the one. In the United States it also fits the modern pattern of Ka- names such as Kamiya and Kamaya.
A respelling of Desiree or of the word desire. Desiree is French Désirée, desired, from the Latin name Desiderata.
A Yiddish pet form of Shaina, from sheyn, beautiful, with the diminutive ending -del.
A respelling of Niles, an English surname meaning son of Niel or Neil, the medieval form of the Irish name Niall.
A modern American name that joins Ry-, as in Ryan and Rylee, to the -lyn ending. For boys it is also a spelling of Rylan.
A respelling of Amelia, which comes from the Germanic element amal, work or vigor, and was later confused with the Roman family name Aemilia.
From Sanskrit anagha, without sin: the negative prefix an- with agha, fault or sin. It is also a name of the goddess Lakshmi.
A German occupational surname for a maker or mender of kettles and copper pots, from Kessel, kettle.
A combination of May and Lynn, in the same family as Maelyn and Raelynn.
A recent spelling found mostly in Spanish-speaking families, close to Sheyla and Sheila.
A recent name with the -lyn ending on an Ed- opening, as in Eden and Edith. It is close in sound to Adelyn and Evelyn.
A -lyn spelling of Lachlan or Lochlan, a Scottish name from Gaelic Lochlann, land of the lochs, an old name for Norway and the Vikings who came from it.
The Hindi form of Sanskrit moksha, release: in Hindu, Jain and Buddhist thought, freedom from the cycle of death and rebirth.
The Spanish word for butterfly, traditionally explained as Mari, pósate: Mary, alight.
A spelling of Raya. Raya is used in several languages, among them as a Russian short form of Raisa, and it rose in the United States after Disney's 2021 film Raya and the Last Dragon.
